https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/how-.text: The tunnel was uncovered by Latvian authorities in early August. Latvia faces an increasing number of migrants trying to cross the border from Belarus, further straining relations between the two countries. Latvia shares a 173km border with Belarus. Latvia is a member of the European Union. Belarus, an independent nation with an authoritarian government, is not. At the time of the tunnel's discovery, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said criminal networks were facilitating migration from Belarus into Latvia, bringing migrants into Europe's borderless Schengen area, but that the migrants' final destination was elsewhere on the continent. "They migrate to where it's easier (to enter the EU). So we must not be the easiest place," Kulbergs told the press conference. He pledged to target networks transporting the migrants from the border to their destinations, as well as any support points for migrants in Latvia, as part of what he called "Operation Werewolf". "If everything goes according to plan, we are confident that we will already deal a serious enough blow to the system," Kulbergs said. "I want to tell the organisers: everything will be put to an end." Latvia's government said in a statement it would cooperate with neighbours Estonia, Lithuania, Poland and others to stop the flow of migrants. Latvia, along with Lithuania and Poland, has frequently accused Belarus' authoritarian government of smuggling migrants from crisis-impacted regions close to the EU's far borders. Having now discovered a second tunnel at another point along the border fence, Latvia is pointing fingers at the Belarusian border guard. "It is simply impossible to build such a tunnel without the Belarusian border guards being aware of it," Guntis Pujats, head of the agency, told Latvian radio on Thursday. Pujats went on to give more information about the original tunnel, saying that the entrance on the Belarusian side of the border was found around 10m from the border line and had been hidden among trees and bushes. The tunnel itself was reported to be 80cm wide and to run for roughly 30m. Some 28 cubic metres of earth had been removed to construct the tunnel. Support structures had been erected within the tunnel to keep it from collapsing, and a plywood cover had been fitted to the entrance. "The construction work was quite extensive. So the relevant authorities were undoubtedly aware of it," he said. Pujats claimed that 12 underground tunnels have been found across Lithuania, along with the two found in Latvia to date. The Belarusian government has not publicly commented on the existence of the tunnels. download our app subscribe to our newsletter

Photograph: Andrea de Silva/Reuters View image in fullscreen Messiah Burnley, nephew of Chad Joseph, who family members believe was killed in a US military strike on a boat in the Caribbean, carries a girl in front of an altar for Joseph in the family home in Las Cuevas, Trinidad and Tobago, on 22 October 2025. Photograph: Andrea de Silva/Reuters United Nations US strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN expert says Dozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025 Tiago Rogero , South America correspondent Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.54 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”. The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean. The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further. In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC , Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”. He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.” The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks. US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”. As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking. Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”. The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US. “Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added. The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment. Although Trump recently claimed the bombings had stopped 97% of all illegal drugs entering the US by sea, according to available data , the attacks have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the US. Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims , who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, were at best low-ranked participants in trafficking networks. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/mi.text: The horrific way a man was killed after being abducted in Birmingham has been revealed in court. Four men have been handed sentences for the killing of a member of an organised crime gang who was tortured, doused in petrol and set on fire. Tomasz Samel, 45, was abducted in 2019 in Birmingham by three men posing as Interpol officers, before being driven to the Liverpool area and subjected to a brutal attack over the loss of cigarettes valued at £1 million. Read more: Healthy police officer dies In August, a jury unanimously found Neil Jones, 49, of no fixed address, and Tobiasz Kozlowski, 38, of Kirkby, Merseyside, guilty of Mr Samel's murder and conspiracy to cause grievous bodily harm. Fellow defendants Kevin Wooden, 46, of Banbury, Oxfordshire, and Kye Arthur, 35, of Lockleaze, Bristol, were convicted of manslaughter. Kozlowski's wife, Sandra Kozlowska, 38, also of Kirkby, was found guilty of assisting an offender by aiding him in evading detection by police. On Friday, Jones was handed a life sentence with a minimum term of 34 years, while Kozlowski also received a life sentence with a minimum tariff of 33 years. Wooden was sentenced to 23 years behind bars, while Arthur received a 22-year prison term. Kozlowska was given a three-year sentence, suspended for three years. Mr Justice Wall told the defendants at Birmingham Crown Court : "You all chose to involve yourselves in a truly horrific series of events. "The motive for this was that he was in possession of a consignment of cigarettes worth £1 million illegally imported from Poland, when they were seized by HMRC . "He was held responsible for their loss. Following his kidnap, Mr Samel was detained in the Liverpool area for some time. "It is impossible to say how he was treated during the early part of his detention because the extent of his later-inflicted burn injuries did not allow for his body to be examined for other marks of violence. "I do not sentence you on the basis that he was tortured during this time. However, this lengthy period of detention must have been terrifying for him. "After a number of hours of detention, he was stripped naked, and, while seated and defenceless, petrol was thrown over him and he was set alight. "He suffered extensive burns to most of his body. He was then dressed and driven to a remote area where he was thrown out of a vehicle onto the side of the road. "His injuries were so serious that anyone who saw him after they were inflicted and chose to leave him without assistance of any kind must have intended that he would die of them." The cigarettes, which had been unlawfully smuggled in from Poland, had been in Mr Samel's possession – stored in a unit in Aston, Birmingham – at the time they were seized by HM Revenue and Customs on February 22 2019. Mr Samel, who was the subject of an international arrest warrant, was abducted from his residence on Raleigh Road, Handsworth, at approximately 8.35am on March 27, 2019. Following his placement in a white van, he was transported to Merseyside before being abandoned in an isolated area near Bickerstaffe in Lancashire, where he sought assistance at a property at 11.10pm that evening . The judge noted that the descriptions of Mr Samel's injuries by attending paramedics and those who saw him at the scene were "harrowing and disturbing". "He was in hospital for almost three months before he died," the judge said. "The level of his suffering between the time at which the injuries were inflicted and his death is difficult to imagine." Mr Samel passed away at Whiston Hospital in Prescot on 21 June 2019 , due to his injuries. The judge characterised the scheme as a "carefully executed plan" and identified Koslowski and Jones as the "organisers" of what befell Mr Samel, given their financial interest in the confiscated cigarettes. He informed the court he was certain that Koslowski was present when Mr Samel was set alight but could not determine whether he "lit the flame". "There might have been others in Poland or in this country who also played a role in the organisation of these events," the judge continued. "It might be that they were able to exert some pressure on you to do what you did. But any organisational involvement by others does not diminish your responsibility for what happened." The judge stated Wooden and Arthur were hired to abduct Mr Samel, alongside a third individual who remains unidentified, and at first pretended to be Amazon delivery drivers before claiming to be law enforcement officers. He informed the court there was a "very high degree of mental and physical suffering inflicted" on Mr Samel prior to his death. Kozlowski and Jones entered guilty pleas to conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison ahead of the trial commencing. Jones had also admitted manslaughter. Wooden and Arthur acknowledged conspiracy to kidnap and conspiracy to falsely imprison. Following the case, Kate Seal, of the Crown Prosecution Service, commented: "This was a sustained and merciless attack on a man taken from the safety of his own home. "Bringing all those responsible to justice required years of painstaking work, including close co-operation with West Midlands Police and international partners across three countries, to gather the forensic, digital and witness evidence needed to secure these convictions. "Mr Samel's family have shown extraordinary strength throughout this ordeal. "Our thoughts remain with them, and I hope these sentences reflect the severity of what was inflicted on Mr Samel and provide the family with a sense of justice being achieved, though nothing can undo their loss." The police inquiry prompted extensive investigations across Poland, Greece , the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Colombia, France, Scotland and Wales, where the criminal network had either established operations or sought refuge following the abduction.

Newsflash Newsroom , 17.10.2026, 19:30 Summit. France has offered to help Romania with equipment to ensure security in the Black Sea, President Nicușor Dan announced after the European summit held on Friday in Brussels. The offer comes as an increasing number of commercial vessels in the Black Sea are being targeted by drones. Nicușor Dan explained that Bucharest had requested support from its allies, just like it did nearly a year ago in response to security incidents along the Danube. “Romania has allies, and in times of need, we receive their help, and, of course, there is the SAFE program, which, once the contracts are finalized, will provide permanent, definitive protection in the Black Sea,” he added. At the Brussels summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the war would continue to exert immense pressure on his country, as Russia intensifies its attacks on cities and energy infrastructure. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said funding for Ukraine in 2026 is secured, but that the needs for 2027 will require the mobilization of additional resources and contributions from other international partners. In this context, EU heads of state and government requested that the European Commission put forward a proposal to address Ukraine’s additional financing needs for the coming year, needs which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has estimated at 70 billion euros. Government. Luca Niculescu’s proposed ministers will be heard by the relevant parliamentary committees early next week, with the investiture vote scheduled for Tuesday afternoon during a joint session of the Parliament in Bucharest. This decision follows the submission of the governing program and the list of cabinet members to Parliament by the Prime Minister-designate on Thursday. Of the 17 proposed ministers, 11 are from the Social Democratic Party, while 6 are independents. If all the parties and groups that have announced their support vote for the new government in Parliament, the 233 votes needed with be exceeded On Saturday, the Liberal leader Ilie Bolojan announced that his party, which will move into opposition, would support the new government through a “conditional and specific vote of necessity,” following the signing of an agreement with the prime minister-designate on Monday. Support will also come from the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania, with its leader Kelemen Hunor saying the party will vote for the government regardless of its membership. Previously, the national minorities group and the “United for Romania” group had also indicated their support. On the other hand, the Save Romania Union and the Alliance for the Union of Romanians will not vote for the new government. Drones. Two drones that entered the national airspace were shot down over Romania’s territorial waters, the Ministry of Defence in Bucharest announced on Saturday. According to the Ministry, F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force were scrambled after radar surveillance systems detected a group of aerial targets moving approximately 120 kilometers east of Snake Island, in the Black Sea. On Friday night, the Ministry of Defence’s radar surveillance system detected another aerial target moving over Ukrainian territory toward the border with Romania, in the northern part of Tulcea County (eastern Romania). Two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Force were scrambled. No incursions into the national airspace were reported, the Ministry of Defence said. EU funding. Romania still has 6.43 billion euros worth of National Recovery and Resilience Plan funding to receive, which are essential for meeting the budget deficit target, the Ministry of Finance said in a statement. He warns that any expenditures on projects whose objectives and milestones are not approved by the European Commission will have to be covered by the national budget. Of the remaining amount, 2.08 billion euros are linked to the fifth payment request, which is currently under evaluation, while the rest is requested via the final payment request, the sixth, submitted at the end of last month. The European Commission’s decision is expected by November 20. To date, Romania has received 13.27 billion euros under the recovery and resilience facility, accounting for some two-thirds of the Plan’s total value.
